video_title: What Buffett Saw in Japan That Investors Missed | Global Macro | Ep.109
gist: Andrew McDermott of Mission Value Partners argues Japan's competence-based capitalism, industrial depth and sound balance sheet are undervalued by a Western investment industry captured by financialization and a China narrative; Buffett's all-in Japan allocation is his key evidence. He is skeptical of US AI capex and flags Japan turning into 'KKR's portfolio' as the main risk.

insights.claim: Andrew McDermott of Mission Value Partners argues Japan's capitalism works better because it is organized around competence at making things, whereas the US is organized around compensation for financiers.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Frames the case for structurally overweighting Japanese industrials versus financialized Western markets.
insights.quote: the through line in in terms of what makes Japan capitalism work is that it is organized around competence

insights.claim: McDermott dates the US shift away from making things to KKR's takeover of Houdaille around 1980, which he says helped bankrupt the American machine tool industry and set the leveraged-buyout template later applied across Europe outside Germany.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Narrative that private-equity financialization hollowed out industrial capacity is the root of his bullishness on Japanese toolmakers.

insights.claim: McDermott claims Japan's corporate governance model is the same one that worked in the US from World War II to 1980 (promoted insiders, resilience over stated ROIC), and that the worst governance failures of 30 years were American, European or Chinese, not Japanese.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Challenges the standard 'Japan must reform governance' thesis behind many Japan allocations.

insights.claim: He argues the Japan-changing narrative reflects more on the Western investment industry than on Japan, and that Shinzo Abe's reforms were not the cause: companies changed to survive as cross-holdings unwound over 40 years.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Reform-driven Japan trades premised on top-down policy may misread the actual driver, which is corporate competitive pressure.

insights.claim: McDermott says Berkshire Hathaway is the most Japanese company in America in every sense, including governance, and that Japanese conglomerates already do what Musk is trying to build by integrating spaceships, phone spectrum and turbine blades.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Supports conglomerate structures as a durable model rather than a discount-worthy inefficiency.
insights.quote: Berkshire Hathaway is the most Japanese company in America in every sense

insights.claim: McDermott says Warren Buffett ignored Japan for roughly 50 years and then went all in just when the investment industry gave up, and that Buffett's international allocation is now 100% Japan.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Buffett's concentration in Japanese trading houses is a contrarian signal against consensus China-centric EM allocations.
insights.quote: Warren Buffett's international allocation right now is 100% Japan

insights.claim: John Templeton held about 75% in Japan in 1974 when Japan was about 12% of global markets and cut it to half in 1975, per McDermott; he notes Japan was once about 55% of global markets, so its roughly 6% MSCI World weight is historically low.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Historic allocations suggest current index weight understates Japan's potential if sentiment normalizes.

insights.claim: McDermott says that in 1998 Buffett dismissed Japan as having terrible returns and management, and that the surviving Japanese companies have since competed for talent and capital and improved without being forced to by activists.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Explains why Buffett's change of view is about company quality rather than a macro call.

insights.claim: McDermott warns that foreign shareholders own about 35% of the Japanese market yet mostly care more about China, and that his biggest risk is Japan becoming more like KKR's portfolio rather than China becoming more like Japan.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Key downside: financialization of Japanese corporates via activists and private equity could erode the model that makes them valuable.
insights.quote: not that China becomes more like Japan, but that Japan becomes more like KKR's portfolio

insights.claim: GPIF, the roughly $1.3 trillion Japanese pension fund, invests in public markets with about 200 staff, two basis points of fees and no private equity, with around 40% equities of which about 25% Japanese per McDermott's recollection.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: A low-cost, public-market, staff-light model has done well and contrasts with the private-equity-heavy Western pensions.

insights.claim: McDermott says Japanese investment in his home state of Tennessee and the US Southeast exceeds $20 billion across steel, rare earths, power generation machinery, nuclear power plants and automated manufacturing, much of it replacing items previously made in China.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Evidence that reshoring is flowing through Japanese capex and suppliers.

insights.claim: He says Japanese machine tool orders hit a record last month in both the US and China, reversing decades of decline in US demand.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: A leading indicator of capex cycle in manufacturing that benefits Japanese toolmakers such as Okuma.

insights.claim: McDermott argues that no gas turbine sold by GE is not actually forged in Japan, because GE and Westinghouse stopped making components, so the AI-driven power buildout creates demand for Japanese industrial capacity.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Power and turbine bottlenecks give pricing power to Japanese heavy-industry suppliers.

insights.claim: He argues the low-rates, low-inflation era rested on false price signals from China suppressing rates and prices, citing rare earth prices and General Motors' China profits (GM wrote off $6 billion in China), and that those signals are now reversing.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Supports a regime view of higher structural capital demand and a repricing of strategic inputs like rare earth magnets.

insights.claim: McDermott observes that manufacturing jobs rose strongly in the last US jobs report while finance jobs declined, and that private equity and private credit are struggling to generate deal flow.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Anecdotal sign of capital rotating from financial engineering to physical capacity.

insights.claim: He says higher interest rates are not hurting Japan because it has become a growth market with rising demand for robots, rare earths, nuclear plants and semiconductors, and that the world now needs more capital rather than less.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Japan equities as a beneficiary rather than a casualty of a higher-rate, higher-capital-demand regime.

insights.claim: McDermott calls most current AI spending a gigantic negative return on invested capital visible on company balance sheets and a misallocation of human capital comparable to the financial sector, while doubting five or six tech leaders' spending without revenue represents leadership.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Bearish stance on US AI capex returns, with preference for AI's industrial applications.

insights.claim: He claims Japan leads in economically productive AI, namely machine learning applied to continuous improvement of manufacturing, and that his two largest holdings were discussing it by 2015-2016.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Positions Japanese manufacturers and robotics as AI beneficiaries not priced as AI plays.

insights.claim: He cites Anduril wanting a drone with no Chinese parts and finding the only way was in Japan with 100% Japanese parts, as evidence of Japan's supply chain depth.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Defense and non-China supply chains favor Japanese component makers.

insights.claim: McDermott says Japan is quietly the primary market on which AI models train, referencing a piece by Jesper Koll, and says Japan is close to partnering with IBM on 1.5 nanometer technology while TSMC invests aggressively in Japan.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Semiconductor and AI-supporting investment in Japan may broaden the equity story beyond autos.

insights.claim: McDermott rejects the 'Japanification of China' framing, arguing deflation after a real estate debt boom also happened in the US in the 1930s and that Britain and France's deindustrialization fits the label better, and says China has not surpassed Japan at the top of the value chain.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Pushes back on narratives that China is the new hegemon and the template to copy.

insights.claim: He argues Japan's public debt is less alarming on a consolidated basis, citing a Federal Reserve paper that puts US and Japanese governments on an apples-to-apples footing including pensions and assets, finding Japan is not an outlier and its balance sheet structure is favorable.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Counters the standard Japan-debt-bear case; US entitlements are the larger hidden liability.

insights.claim: Japan's pension liabilities were restructured after the Daiko Henjo period (creation of GPIF, benefit cuts, higher retirement age), and benefits are nominal while assets are real, the reverse of the US, which McDermott says holds Social Security in T-bills.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Inflation helps Japan's balance sheet while hurting nominal-asset-heavy systems, and shows capacity for hard fiscal choices.

insights.claim: McDermott says higher JGB yields near 3% raise the relative appeal of domestic bonds versus hedged Treasuries for yield-targeting Japanese investors, and the real question is what happens to other markets, especially France, when Japanese lenders repatriate.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Repatriation from overseas fixed income is a transmission channel for higher global yields.

insights.claim: He says a small change in asset allocation by Japanese investors, as a large net foreign investor, can have major impact on other markets, and that stability or a stronger yen would be a tailwind for Japanese assets.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Watch Japanese portfolio flows and the yen as a global liquidity variable.

insights.claim: McDermott's best-case scenario for 2035 is 'Pax Nipponica', drawn from Clyde Prestowitz's book Japan Restored, with China retrenching and joint China-Japan administration of Taiwan, and he says MIT's new Tokyo partnership is a sign universities are reorienting to Japan.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: Long-horizon optimistic scenario rather than a forecast; depends on US-Japan-India-Korea-Taiwan alignment.

insights.claim: He says Japan has alternatives to the US for investment, notably India, so how much Japan and Korea allocate to the US relative to other Asian partners is an open question.
insights.speaker: Andrew McDermott
insights.so_what: US reshoring depends on foreign capital that has other destinations.
